chapter.title: Coreference
chapter.para: The addon artifacts are org.apache.opennlp.addons:coref, coref-formats, and the optional coref-dl. Only the last requires ONNX at runtime. Evaluation figures below were recorded before migration; the original evaluation harness remains available.

section.title: Document-layer coreference
section.para: CorefAnnotator clusters the mentions of a document into coreference chains without a model, following the entity-centric, precision-ranked sieves of Lee et al. (Computational Linguistics 2013). It requires the sentence, token, POS-tag, and entity layers and provides CorefAnnotator.CHAINS: each annotation covers one mention and carries a CorefMention with a chain id, a kind (entity, nominal, or pronoun), and the index of the entity it came from. Singletons are reported too, so no mention is lost; consumers interested only in links filter by chain size.

Mentions are the entities, the noun phrases from optional ParserAnnotator.PHRASES and ChunkerAnnotator.CHUNKS layers, the personal pronouns, and standalone demonstratives (That was costly). When both phrase layers contain the same span, the parser head is used. A noun phrase headed by an entity extends the entity mention to the complete phrase. Possessors remain separate mentions. Chunks joined by of or and form an additional candidate (the law of negligence, Kim and Lee). Pleonastic it is excluded. The rule sieves do not resolve demonstratives, which mostly point at clauses; a ranker decides them. Each mention carries the number, gender, animacy, and person the text supports, read from pronoun forms, plural tags, name titles, a bundled first-name list built from the public-domain Social Security Administration name tables, and lists of gendered and animate nouns. Nine sieves then run in order of decreasing precision, and each links an anaphor to the first candidate whose cluster passes: exact and relaxed string match, acronym and person-name containment, strict head match with two relaxations, proper and relaxed head match, and pronoun resolution within three sentences under number, gender, animacy, person, and entity type agreement. A name never absorbs a compound such as Kansas City, indefinite and bare common noun phrases are antecedents only, and clusters whose known entity types differ never merge.

First and second person pronouns refer to the speaker and the addressee, so they chain per speaker: the value of an optional CorefAnnotator.SPEAKERS layer covering each mention, or, without one, the narrator outside quotation marks and one speaker per quotation, joined to the person a verb of speech attributes the quotation to.

Given a CorefModel, the annotator ranks instead of applying the head-match and pronoun sieves: after the speaker and string sieves, each remaining mention takes the candidate antecedent the model scores highest. A model from CorefTrainer.trainRanking is a mention ranker after Durrett and Klein (EMNLP 2013), trained by softmax over each mention's candidates and the option of starting a new chain, and links when the best candidate outscores that option; a model from CorefTrainer.train is a pair classifier and links when the best link probability reaches CorefAnnotator.DEFAULT_THRESHOLD. The features are the sieve tests as predicates, head words, mention shapes, distance, attribute pairs, cluster size, speaker equality, their conjunctions, and, when the annotator is given WordVectors, the bucketed cosine similarity of the two heads. Given TokenVectors, an encoder that returns one contextual vector per token of a sentence, each mention also has a span vector and the model adds the bucketed cosine of two span vectors and real-valued features, their elementwise product and absolute difference, and the anaphor's vector for the new-chain option; TokenVectorsDL in opennlp-dl wraps a BERT-style ONNX encoder for that purpose. A vector provider declares its dimension, and CorefModel records the contextual dimension used during training. The annotator rejects a missing or mismatched encoder before inference. Training reads documents that carry the annotator's input layers and a CorefAnnotator.GOLD_CHAINS layer, the gold: counterpart of the chains layer; ConlluCorefDocumentStream in coref-formats reads such documents from CoNLL-U with Entity brackets, the encoding of OntoGUM, the Universal Anaphora releases, and the CorefUD collection, including its rich entity ids and discontinuous mention parts. When a document contains singleton gold entities, training treats its gold layer as complete for that annotation scheme and excludes unmatched detected mentions. This supports corpora that mark selected mention types, such as LitBank, alongside OntoNotes-style data.

CorefScorer computes the MUC, B-cubed, and CEAF metrics and the CoNLL average defined by Pradhan et al. (ACL 2014). Measured with it on the OntoGUM corpus with gold sentences, tokens, and tags, predicted entities and chunks, and the corpus speaker lines, the rule-based annotator scores a CoNLL average of 46.8 on the test split and the mention ranker trained on all OntoGUM training documents scores 50.0. A ranker trained on the 59 CC BY training documents scores 49.4. These results are not directly comparable with the 39.7 that Zhu, Pradhan, and Zeldes (ACL 2021) report for the Stanford deterministic system because that system used fully predicted input. Two Reddit documents per OntoGUM split have redacted text; opennlp.coref.skip.redacted omits them. The harness is OntoGumCorefEvalTest, which also reads CorefUD files. GapCorefEvalTest checks fully predicted input on GAP. The CC BY ranker scores 46.1 development F1 and 45.5 test F1, compared with the GAP paper's reported 50.5 development F1 for Stanford dcoref. CorefPipelineExampleTest asserts the behavior shown here.
